newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tung's vow on no Hong Kong "Tiananmens" welcomed.
newsitem.headline: Tung's vow on no Hong Kong "Tiananmens" welcomed.

text.p: A pledge by Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa guaranteeing no bloody "Tiananmen" crackdowns after China takes over the territory drew calls from his opponents on Wednesday to match words with deeds.
Tung vowed on U.S. ABC News' "Nightline" programme on Tuesday to protect the right to protest and declared there would be no repression in Hong Kong under his leadership.

Images of Chinese tanks crushing a student-led democracy movement centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989 burns vividly in the collective memory of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people. The British colony reverts to China at midnight on June 30.

Tung's remark came on the last day of a pulse-taking exercise tapping public views on his plan to amend civil liberties laws, particularly clauses concerning the right to protest and funding of political groups.
Asked if the Tiananmen crackdown could be repeated in Hong Kong, Tung said: "No, it can't happen here. It will not happen here. I will not allow it to happen here.

"Demonstration is part of our culture, demonstration is part of life...they will be free to demonstrate as they please, but I would hope they would abide by the laws of Hong Kong if they wish to do so," Tung said.
Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, welcomed Tung's comments but urged him to match words with deeds and refrain from rolling back civil liberties.

"This is an encouraging statement from our Chief Executive designate Mr Tung Chee-hwa which recognises the reality that Hong Kong is a free society where people regularly exercise their right to demonstrate peacefully within the law," Lee said.
"But there is a significant discrepancy between what Mr Tung is saying to ("Nightline" host) Ted Koppel and what he has proposed doing."

Governor Chris Patten, who has attacked Tung's proposals on the grounds they would erode civil liberties and provide a dangerous precedent for future amendments of constitutional safeguards, echoed Lee's sentiments.

"I welcome, of course, what Mr Tung said, and I'm sure he meant what he said. But I think it just raises question marks about why there are going to be changes in the law on demonstrations, for example, if nobody is going be stopped from demonstrating," he told reporters.
Tung's proposals include a ban on foreign funding of political groups and making it obligatory to obtain police permission to stage protests seven days in advance of the event.
At present, demonstrators merely have to notify police.
Pro-democracy parties, lawyers, human rights groups, unions and churches were quick to object to Tung's plan in written submissions.
Groups representing industry, commerce, pro-China parties and pro-Beijing trade unions have declared support.
Public appeals by officials seconded to Tung's office for more support for the proposals raised doubts about the authenticity of the consultation process, law professor Nihal Jayawickrama said.
A spokesman for Tung said more than 4,000 submissions had been received by Wednesday evening, including 200 relayed on the Internet to Tung's home page at http://www.ceooffice.org.hk.
Opinion polls have shown Tung's popularity has declined since he made the proposals public but regular surveys show confidence in Hong Kong's post-colonial future to be on the rise.
A poll conducted by television station ATV on Wednesday showed Tung's popularity rating dropped to 57.9 percent in April from 79.2 percent a month earlier.
Patten remains a shade more popular than Tung although his rating also dropped, falling to 58.7 percent from 85.2 percent, ATV said but gave no details.

A University of Hong Kong survey published on Wednesday found that more than 65 percent of 502 respondents were confident about Hong Kong's post-colonial future, an increase of 2.7 percentage points from a previous survey in March.
London and Washington have also opposed the need for change. The human rights group Amnesty International submitted a 17-page set of objections to the measures.
"Amnesty International is concerned that some of the proposed changes would significantly weaken safeguards for human rights in Hong Kong," the London-based group said.
Tung's future Justice Secretary Elsie Leung said she expected the amendments to be drafted into a proposed law by the middle of next month, Radio Hong Kong reported.
